_comment: What we checked after the runs, finding by finding: against the browser's own record (_capture.json), the screenshots, the site's files and, where the finding is about Claude Code, its documentation. A finding is kept whatever the verdict, so the next study can be compared with this one. Verdicts: confirmed; partly (part of it holds, the note says which); artefact (caused by our helper or the method, not the site); not-confirmed (the site does what the finding says it does not).

verdicts.partly: part of it holds; the note says which
verdicts.artefact: caused by our helper or the method, not the site
verdicts.not-confirmed: the site already does what the finding says it does not

helper_changes: clicktext now clicks the first visible match; in S1 it could pick a hidden one (Marcus, step 14)

checks.note: The source is all there, in a box that scrolls: 418 of its 1,246 pixels show, and nothing says it scrolls. What he needed, which files it stops, is not in plain words anywhere on the page.
The matcher names every file tool and Bash, and nothing beside it says the hook answers only when a credential file is named.
No page says how to remove a hook.
Five of five asked what the £50 was.
A still screenshot cannot watch an animation: the demo is typing, not stuck. What holds: measured in the same browser, the refusal appears about eleven seconds after the demo comes into view.
The Docs menu is the brief, the memo and how the site is built.
The first paragraph names a hook and Claude Code; ChatGPT first appears half a page down.
On /policies/ the Claude Code pack and section come first; the ChatGPT section is about 1,500 pixels down on a phone.
As for Sam.
The only stronger control listed for send-as-you is an organisation administrator's setting in Claude, from riskmandate.ai's rule. We do not yet know what a ChatGPT user can set for themselves.
Our generator wrote 'Neither half is a boundary' on pages with only one half.
The home page says the hook stops the read; how it fails is two clicks away.

RM-R0015's page has the same limits table as the others, further down; he reached the page on his last action and saw only its top. What holds: the limit is not at the top, where a reader arrives from the self-edit link.

No page said what happens when a hook cannot run. Claude Code's documentation: any failure other than exit code 2, a timeout included, lets the action go ahead. And the tests feed the hook the JSON Claude Code would send; they do not drive a live session.
As for Sam.
Managed settings are named only in a hook's source comment.
The helper's clicktext matched hidden text first and timed out; the link works, as his next action showed. The helper now clicks the first visible match.
Nothing says that committing .claude/settings.json gives everybody who pulls the same hooks, which Claude Code's documentation says it does.
No page says what joining commits a company to.
RM-R0015 asks the person at the keyboard. For a company, the answer is managed settings, which no page names.
Confirmed that nothing explains it; we are keeping the prices.
The first batch page is the lead's tracking. She went there looking for terms, which are nowhere.
As for Sam.
The settings run python3 and no page says so. On Windows, Claude Code runs hooks in Git Bash, or PowerShell if Git Bash is not installed; a hook that cannot start lets the action through.
Worse than the finding: the instruction is out of date. Claude Code applies changes to hooks in the running session.
Try it gave only the two outcomes.
As for Sam.
The stronger controls read as a second required step; nothing says they are optional.
The status line at the top of start here holds. The dropdown over step 4 was our helper: the mouse stayed where it clicked the menu, and the menu opens on hover.
